primary.thesis: Under these rules only a closure ordered by Israeli authorities counts: a broad shutdown of commercial aviation over all or most of Israeli civilian airspace. Foreign airline suspensions and third-country NOTAMs do not count, and neither do short ground stops or local closures. Israel has ordered closures like this only in direct state-on-state exchanges with Iran. Examples are the April 2024 barrage, the October 2024 missile attack, the June 2025 war, and escalation rounds after that. Houthi missiles, Hezbollah fire and Gaza rockets have produced only short ground stops or local restrictions. The market's existence shows tension is high, but a qualifying closure needs a new, discrete Israel-Iran escalation (an Israeli or US strike on Iran, or a large Iranian salvo) inside the window. Israel usually closes its airspace pre-emptively when it strikes first, so the decision rests with Israel and follows a war decision, not background noise. Over 2 days (C1) that is very unlikely. Over about 2.5 weeks (C2) it is still unlikely unless a trigger is already visible. The 7-week window (C3) is the most exposed rung, so I keep it out of the basket. The expression is NO on the short end of the ladder.

basket.reason: Only 2 days of window. A qualifying closure would need an Israel-Iran strike exchange starting almost at once, and short ground stops from Houthi or Hezbollah fire do not meet the 'major closure' test.

About 18 days. Broad closures by Israeli authorities have followed only a few discrete escalations with Iran each year. Without an announced strike campaign or collapsed talks, the base rate for a new round in under three weeks is low.

failure_narrative: Israel, or the US with Israeli coordination, strikes Iranian nuclear or missile sites before July 31. Possible reasons are stalled nuclear talks, intelligence that Iran is rebuilding enrichment or its missile stockpile, or the end of a ceasefire or deadline. Israel pre-emptively closes Ben Gurion and the national airspace, as in June 2025, and Iran answers with a ballistic-missile salvo. A second path is Iran or a proxy launching a mass drone and missile attack big enough that the Israel Airports Authority suspends all commercial flights nationally, not just for a brief ground stop. In either case the closure is ordered by Israeli authorities and national in scope, so C2 (and C1 if it happens by July 15) resolves YES and both NO legs lose.
hedge_thesis: The worlds where the basket loses are worlds where an Israel-Iran shooting war restarts. That hits Persian Gulf energy flows straight away. Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz faces the risk of Iranian harassment, mining or a closure threat. War-risk insurance premiums for Gulf shipping rise, and traders add a supply-disruption premium to crude. Brent and WTI rise sharply, tanker freight rates jump, and gold rises as a safe haven. The same trigger (a strike on Iran) causes both the Israeli airspace closure and the Gulf energy shock, so a long crude oil or tanker-rate position pays in exactly the worlds where the NO basket fails.
